findings.title: Downloaded native libduckdb is dlopen'd + JIT-linked with no checksum/signature verification
findings.description: The @cres wrappers depend on `duckdb_lib = load_duckdb()` executed at import (ducklib.py:11). On macOS with a C-API-stripped wheel, that call falls through to `_download_libduckdb()` (utils.py:50-91), which does `urlopen(url).read()` (utils.py:83-84), opens it as a zip in memory, extracts the `libduckdb.dylib` member to `~/.numbduck/lib/<version>/libduckdb.dylib` (utils.py:85-89), and then `load_lib_path(...)` dlopens it RTLD_GLOBAL (utils.py:130) so its `duckdb_*` symbols are JIT-linked into every binding. There is NO integrity check on the downloaded bytes: no SHA-256 comparison against a pinned digest, no GPG/codesign signature verification, no Content-Length/size sanity. The version-keyed cache (utils.py:41-43) is likewise reloaded on every subsequent run with no verification, so a single bad/poisoned write to that path is executed as native code thereafter. Because the artifact is a shared library that is loaded and whose symbols are executed, any substitution of the bytes is arbitrary code execution in the host process. TLS (default urlopen cert validation against the GitHub release host) is the ONLY integrity guarantee — there is no defense-in-depth against a compromised release asset, CDN/mirror, or a tampered cache file.
findings.impact: If the downloaded or cached dylib bytes are ever altered (compromised release asset, TLS-bypass/trust-store compromise, or local tampering of the unverified `~/.numbduck/lib/<ver>/` cache), the substituted native code is dlopen'd RTLD_GLOBAL and its symbols JIT-linked into the process, i.e. arbitrary code execution under the user's identity. Mitigating factors lower the likelihood: macOS-only path, requires a C-API-stripped wheel, requires consent (NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 or an interactive 'y'), and TLS protects the transport.
findings.recommendation: Pin and verify before loading: ship a per-version SHA-256 (and ideally the upstream release's published digest/signature) and compare `hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()` against it before extracting; refuse to load on mismatch. Re-verify the cached file's digest on each `_find_standalone_libduckdb()` hit, not just at download time, so a tampered cache entry is rejected. Optionally verify the macOS code signature (`codesign --verify`) of the extracted dylib.

notes: Scope note: the @cres wrappers themselves (ducklib.py:275-1432) are SOUND from a security standpoint. Every wrapper is a thin 1:1 FFI forwarder, e.g. `duckdb_bind_blob` (294-296), `duckdb_create_blob` (636-638), `duckdb_bind_varchar_length` (408-410), `duckdb_create_varchar_length` (606-608), all of which forward the (data_p, length) and (val_p, length) pairs verbatim to libduckdb. Forwarding length/pointer args raw is NOT a defect here: it is the irreducible contract of an FFI binding (and of the DuckDB C API, whose duckdb_bind_blob/create_blob/bind_varchar_length signatures themselves take (const void*, idx_t length) on trust). The binding layer cannot validate the extent of a bare `intp` pointer, and the @njit caller owns pointer/length validity exactly as a C caller would; a wrong/oversized length causing OOB in libduckdb is a caller bug identical to calling the C symbol directly. Length/size args are correctly typed `uint64` to match `idx_t` (e.g. signatures at 79, 103, 110, 154), so there is no signed/unsigned truncation that would silently turn a benign value into an OOB length. The error-handling contract is upheld: every wrapper does `return _call_lib_func(...)` and never raises into C (the only raises are `cres_if_available` Python-time stubs at 725/1050/1284 for genuinely-absent symbols, outside the @njit path). Env-var override `NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB` (utils.py:34) loads a user-specified path — deliberate user override, not a vuln. Zip extraction (utils.py:88) uses a hardcoded member name `libduckdb.dylib` written to a fixed dest, so there is no zip-slip/path-traversal. The single reported finding lives in utils.py but is reachable through this unit's import side effect at ducklib.py:11; if a dedicated loader/utils SEC review unit exists it may overlap and should own the deeper loader analysis (double-load of two runtimes, handle-retention, single-symbol presence heuristic) which is out of scope for the wrappers.
